titre: The Venus de Milo: A Date That Was Made to Disappear
accroche: In 1820, an inscribed base was found with the statue discovered at Melos. It dated the work three centuries later than claimed. It has disappeared.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 8, 1820, on the Greek island of Melos, a farmer digging in the ruins of an ancient theater uncovers a marble statue in several pieces. A French naval officer visiting the island, Olivier Voutier, witnesses the find and encourages the man to keep digging. The statue's arms are already missing; a hand holding an apple and arm fragments are found nearby, though no one has ever been able to link them to the body with certainty. The long-repeated legend of a brawl between French and Turkish sailors that supposedly broke off the arms during transport does not hold up: a sketch of the statue made before it left the island already shows it without arms.

## A base that would have changed everything

Among the fragments found near the statue is a third batch of marble, including a base. Set against the statue's left side, it fits perfectly. A drawing made at the time by Auguste Debay, the only surviving record of it, shows that it bore a carved inscription: a dedication reconstructed as "[...]andros, son of Menides, citizen of Antioch on the Meander, made this statue." Antioch on the Meander was founded only after 280 BCE, which would place the work in the Hellenistic period, three centuries after the classical age of Phidias and Praxiteles to which it was being linked.

France had just lost its Venus de' Medici, returned to Italy in 1815 after Napoleon's fall, and was looking for a centerpiece to fill its place at the Louvre. The Comte de Forbin, the museum's director, judges that this base does not belong to the statue, dismissing it as a clumsy later restoration, and has the scholar Quatremère de Quincy publish a 1821 memoir placing the work in the classical period. This remains the Louvre's official position for more than a hundred and thirty years. The inscribed base itself disappears from the museum's holdings; no one ever explains what became of it.

## A dating recovered by another path

The base's disappearance proves neither that it belonged to the statue nor that it did not: some art historians, including a former chief curator of Greek antiquities at the Louvre, now doubt the link between the two, since Debay's drawing does not show where the missing left foot would have rested. But the later dating eventually prevailed by another route. In 1893, the German archaeologist Adolf Furtwängler established it through stylistic comparison alone, later confirmed by the 1877 discovery, on the same island, of a Hellenistic statue of Poseidon of very similar style. The Venus de Milo, one of the most famous Greek works in the world, is therefore not from the classical age long attributed to it. And the one piece of evidence that could have revealed this as early as 1820 has disappeared, without anyone knowing whether it was because it was inconvenient, or simply because it was lost.

repere.texte: An inscribed base, found with the statue in 1820 and later lost, named a sculptor active after 280 BCE, three centuries after the classical age to which the work was assigned. The Hellenistic dating eventually prevailed in 1893, by another route, without this base.
repere.source: Smithsonian Magazine, "Base Deception," Gregory Curtis, 2003; Wikipedia, "Venus de Milo"

carte.punch: The Venus de Milo arrived with a base that aged it by three centuries. It has disappeared.
carte.idee: Discovered at Melos in 1820, the Venus de Milo arrived with an inscribed base that would date it to the Hellenistic period, three centuries after the classical age the Louvre wanted to link it to. The base disappeared; the later dating was confirmed in 1893 by another route.

quiz.question: What does the disappearance of the inscribed base found with the Venus de Milo in 1820 change about its history?
choix: It prevents us from knowing whether the statue depicts Aphrodite or another goddess
It prevents us from proving that this base belonged to the statue, and so from confirming its dating by the inscription
It proves that the entire statue is a fake made in the twentieth century
It prevents us from knowing whether the arms were lost before or after the discovery
quiz.explication: The lost base can neither prove nor rule out that it belonged to the statue, since it no longer exists to be examined. The Hellenistic dating accepted today comes from elsewhere, from stylistic comparisons made in 1893, independent of this base.
